units.title: Hello, Kotlin
units.summary: Write your first Kotlin program with fun main and println, and print text and numbers.

lesson.md: Every Kotlin program starts in a function called `main`. You write it as `fun main()`, followed by curly braces `{ }`. The code between the braces runs from top to bottom.
`println` prints a value and then starts a new line. Text in double quotes, like `"Hello"`, is called a **string**. You do not need a semicolon at the end of a line.
`print` prints without starting a new line. The next output continues on the same line. A `println` ends the line.

Numbers do not need quotes. Kotlin calculates with `+`, `-`, `*` and `/`. It calculates the result first and then prints it. As in mathematics, `*` and `/` come before `+` and `-`, and parentheses come first.

lesson.code:
fun main() {
    println(2 + 3)
    println(10 - 4)
    println(6 * 7)
    println(2 + 3 * 4)
    println((2 + 3) * 4)
}

lesson.md: When you divide two whole numbers with `/`, Kotlin drops the rest: `7 / 2` is `3`. The operator `%` gives you the rest of a division. Write `7.0 / 2` to get `3.5`.
`"5"` with quotes is a string, `5` without quotes is a number. For strings, `+` joins the text, so `"2" + "3"` is `23`.

units.title: val, var and types
units.summary: Store values with val and var, and meet the types Int, Double, String and Boolean.

lesson.md: A **variable** is a name for a value. You create one with `val`, a name, `=` and a value. After that, you can use the name instead of the value.
A `val` can never get a new value. If you need a value that changes, use `var`. You give it a new value with `=` again.

lesson.code:
fun main() {
    var score = 10
    println(score)
    score = 15
    println(score)
    score = score + 5
    println(score)
}

lesson.md: Giving a `val` a new value is an error, and the program does not compile. Use `val` by default, and `var` only when the value must change.

Every value has a **type**. `Int` is a whole number, `Double` is a number with a decimal point, `String` is text and `Boolean` is `true` or `false`. Kotlin finds the type from the value. This is called **type inference**.

lesson.code:
fun main() {
    val count = 3
    val price = 2.5
    val city = "Lima"
    val open = true
    println(count)
    println(price)
    println(city)
    println(open)
}

lesson.md: You can also write the type yourself, after the name and a colon: `val count: Int = 3`. A variable keeps its type: an `Int` variable can never hold a string. When you multiply an `Int` by a `Double`, the result is a `Double`.
Short forms change a `var` in place: `x += 2` means `x = x + 2`, and `x -= 2` means `x = x - 2`. `x++` adds `1` and `x--` subtracts `1`.

lesson.code:
fun main() {
    var steps = 0
    steps += 5
    steps++
    println(steps)
    steps -= 2
    println(steps)
}

lesson.md: To turn a value into another type, use functions like `toDouble()`, `toInt()` and `toString()`. `toInt()` on a `Double` drops the decimal part. `toInt()` on a string like `"42"` gives the number `42`.

lesson.code:
fun main() {
    val a = 7
    println(a.toDouble())
    val b = 9.99
    println(b.toInt())
    val text = "42"
    println(text.toInt() + 1)
}

units.title: Strings and templates
units.summary: Build text with string templates and work with length, uppercase() and substring().

lesson.md: You can join strings with `+`. Kotlin also has a shorter way: a **string template**. Write `$` and a variable name inside a string, and Kotlin puts in the value.

lesson.code:
fun main() {
    val name = "Sam"
    val age = 20
    println("Hello, " + name + "!")
    println("Hello, $name!")
    println("$name is $age years old.")
}
lesson.output:
Hello, Sam!
Hello, Sam!
Sam is 20 years old.

lesson.md: For a calculation or anything longer than a name, use curly braces: `${a + b}`. Kotlin runs the code inside the braces and puts the result into the string.
`length` tells you how many characters a string has. Spaces count too. `uppercase()` and `lowercase()` return the string in capital or small letters.

lesson.code:
fun main() {
    val word = "Kotlin"
    println(word.length)
    println(word.uppercase())
    println(word.lowercase())
    println("Hi there".length)
}

lesson.md: The characters are numbered from `0`, so `word[0]` is the first character. `substring(start, end)` returns the part from `start` up to `end`, without `end`. With only `start`, it goes to the end of the string.

lesson.code:
fun main() {
    val word = "Kotlin"
    println(word[0])
    println(word.substring(0, 3))
    println(word.substring(3))
    println(word[word.length - 1])
}

lesson.md: Because `end` is not included, `substring(1, 4)` has `4 - 1 = 3` characters.
Strings have many more functions. `trim()` removes spaces at both ends, `contains` checks for a part, `replace` swaps text and `reversed()` turns the string around.

lesson.code:
fun main() {
    val text = "  I like tea  "
    val clean = text.trim()
    println(clean)
    println(clean.contains("tea"))
    println(clean.replace("tea", "coffee"))
    println("abc".reversed())
}
lesson.output:
I like tea
true
I like coffee
cba

lesson.md: A string never changes. Functions like `uppercase()` return a **new** string. To keep the result, store it in a variable: `val loud = word.uppercase()`.

units.title: Decisions
units.summary: Make decisions with if, else and when, and combine comparisons with &&, || and !.

lesson.md: A comparison gives a `Boolean`: `true` or `false`. Kotlin has `==` (equal), `!=` (not equal), `<` (less than), `>` (greater than), `<=` and `>=`.

lesson.code:
fun main() {
    val age = 17
    println(age >= 18)
    println(age == 17)
    println(age != 17)
    println("cat" == "cat")
}

lesson.md: `if` runs a block of code only when a condition is `true`. The condition goes in parentheses. The `else` block is optional: it runs when the condition is `false`.
With `else if` you can check more conditions, one after the other. Kotlin runs the first block whose condition is `true` and skips the rest.
In Kotlin, `if` also gives back a value. You can store this value in a variable. In this case, the `else` part is required, because the variable needs a value in every case.

lesson.code:
fun main() {
    val a = 8
    val b = 5
    val max = if (a > b) a else b
    println(max)
    val label = if (max % 2 == 0) "even" else "odd"
    println(label)
}

lesson.md: `when` compares one value with many options. Each branch has a value, an arrow `->` and a result. Several values can share a branch, separated by commas. `else` handles all other values. Like `if`, `when` can give back a value.

Without a value after `when`, every branch has its own condition, and the first true one wins. To combine conditions, use **logical operators**: `&&` (and) is `true` when both sides are true, `||` (or) when at least one side is true, and `!` (not) turns `true` into `false`.

lesson.code:
fun main() {
    val age = 25
    val hasTicket = true
    println(age >= 18 && hasTicket)
    println(age < 12 || age > 65)
    println(!hasTicket)
}

units.title: Loops and ranges
units.summary: Repeat code with for loops over ranges like 1..5, until, step and downTo, and with while loops.

lesson.md: A **range** is a sequence of numbers. `1..5` means `1`, `2`, `3`, `4`, `5`: both ends are included. A `for` loop runs its block once for every number in the range. The variable `i` holds the current number.
`until` leaves out the end: `0 until 3` means `0`, `1`, `2`. You can also write it as `0..<3`. This is useful when you count from `0`.
`step` jumps by more than one: `1..9 step 4` means `1`, `5`, `9`. `downTo` counts backwards: `3 downTo 1` means `3`, `2`, `1`. You can combine them.
A loop often updates a variable. Here `sum` starts at `0`, and every round adds the current number to it.
A `for` loop also works with a string. It goes through the characters one by one.
A `while` loop repeats as long as its condition is `true`. It checks the condition before every round. Make sure that the condition becomes `false` at some point, or the loop never ends.
`continue` skips the rest of the current round and goes on with the next one. `break` stops the whole loop at once.

units.title: Functions
units.summary: Write your own functions with parameters, return types, default values and named arguments.

lesson.md: A **function** is a block of code with a name. You can run it again and again. You define it with `fun`, a name, parentheses and a block. You call it with its name and `()`.
**Parameters** pass values into a function. Each parameter has a name and a type, like `name: String`. When you call the function, you pass the values in the same order.
A function can give back a result with `return`. Write the type of the result after the parentheses, like `: Int`. The caller can use the result like any other value.
When a function only returns one expression, you can write it with `=`. Then you leave out the braces and `return`. Kotlin can infer the return type.
A parameter can have a **default value**, like `greeting: String = "Hello"`. If the caller leaves it out, Kotlin uses the default value.

With **named arguments**, you write the parameter name in the call, like `price = 3.5`. This makes calls easier to read. You can also skip a parameter with a default value, and you can pass the arguments in any order.

units.title: Lists, sets and maps
units.summary: Store many values in lists, sets and maps, and transform lists with map and filter.

lesson.md: A **list** holds many values in a fixed order. You create one with `listOf`. Indexes start at `0`, so `fruits[0]` is the first element. `size` tells you how many elements there are, and the last index is `size - 1`.

lesson.code:
fun main() {
    val fruits = listOf("apple", "banana", "cherry")
    println(fruits)
    println(fruits[0])
    println(fruits.size)
    println(fruits.last())
}

lesson.md: A list from `listOf` cannot change. If you want to add, remove or replace elements, create it with `mutableListOf`.

lesson.code:
fun main() {
    val tasks = mutableListOf("read", "write")
    tasks.add("sleep")
    tasks.remove("read")
    tasks[0] = "code"
    println(tasks)
    println(tasks.contains("sleep"))
}

lesson.md: A `for` loop goes through every element of a list, in order. Lists also have ready-made functions like `sum()`, `max()` and `sorted()`.
`map` creates a new list by changing every element. `filter` creates a new list with only the elements that match a condition. Inside the braces, `it` stands for the current element.
A **set** stores every value only once, so duplicates are ignored. Use `setOf`, or `mutableSetOf` for a set that can change. The operator `in` checks if a value is in a collection.
A **map** stores pairs of a key and a value. You create a pair with `to`. `ages["Ben"]` gives you the value for the key `"Ben"`. A `for` loop with `(name, age)` goes through all pairs.

units.title: Classes and null safety
units.summary: Create your own types with class and data class, and handle missing values safely with ?, ?., ?: and !!.

lesson.md: A **class** describes your own type. Its properties go into the parentheses after the class name: `val` for a property that never changes, `var` for one that can change. You create an **object** by calling the class like a function.
A function inside a class is called a **method**. It can use the properties of the object. You call it with a dot, like `room.area()`.

A `data class` is a class for holding data. Kotlin adds useful features: `println` shows the values, `==` compares the values, and `copy` creates a copy with some values changed. For a normal class, `==` only checks if both names point to the same object.

lesson.code:
data class Point(val x: Int, val y: Int)

fun main() {
    val a = Point(1, 2)
    val b = Point(1, 2)
    println(a)
    println(a == b)
    val c = a.copy(y = 5)
    println(c)
}

lesson.md: `null` means "no value". In Kotlin, a normal type like `String` can never be `null`. If a variable may have no value, add a question mark to the type: `String?` is a **nullable** type.

You cannot write `b.length` when `b` is nullable. The **safe call** `?.` gives `null` instead of an error when the value is `null`. The **Elvis operator** `?:` gives a default value when the left side is `null`.

lesson.code:
fun main() {
    val a: String? = "Kotlin"
    val b: String? = null
    println(a?.length)
    println(b?.length)
    println(b?.length ?: 0)
    val name = b ?: "Guest"
    println("Hello, $name")
}

lesson.md: `!!` tells Kotlin: "I am sure that this is not `null`." If the value is `null` anyway, the program stops with a `NullPointerException`. Use `?.` and `?:` when you can.
